title: Hedra and the Lost Stars
markdown:
In the high meadows, before the Midsummer Banner had ever needed saving, Hedra kept sheep and Rowan the stag beetle kept Hedra. They were not siblings by blood. They were siblings by road. Light of my light, she called him, when the flock scattered and only his shell found the stray.

Midsummer drew near. Atop the highest peak the Banner unfurled, woven of moonlight and long daylight, and upon its folds rested three brass stars, the heartbeats of summer’s longest day. Twilight came. A terrible quiet followed. The stars were gone, leaving empty cloth. In the village below, disappointment spread like a dimming; without the stars the festival would go dark.

Hedra, in a quiet meadow, felt the old unease. Rowan nudged her palm.

“The stars are lost,” she said. “The festival will be dark.”

He promised with antennae: they would face it together. Light of my light. Though her knees trembled, she would not let the longest day go blind.

“The old songs speak of the Whispering Hills,” she said. “Perhaps their hearts remember.”

She set Rowan in a pouch at her belt and turned toward the darkening slopes.

The first trial was the Shimmering Stream, a ribbon of water alive with odd light, as if the hills had spilled a piece of sky. Hedra’s fear of being taken under stirred; she had never liked the thought of water closing over her head. Rowan tapped his antennae on the pouch until she looked down. Moss-covered stones made a forgotten path just beneath the shine. She stepped. The stone was slick; her foot wobbled. Fear offered to finish the crossing for her. She pictured the village’s joy, squeezed her eyes, then opened them and took another step, and another. The hill-songs hummed encouragement. She reached the far bank with her heart up and her shoes wet, and she had not gone under.

Deeper in, a grove of willows drooped. Their rustle was so peaceful her eyelids grew heavy, her legs lead. The world blurred. She did not speak. For a stretch of path she only walked, humming a jig without words, Rowan’s weight in the pouch her only conversation, a grounding wriggle when her chin dipped. The cheerful tune pushed the drowsy spell back. Her steps lightened. Her eyes cleared. She marched through the willows’ arms awake, silent toil done, purpose still in her mouth like a held note.

The ascent steepened. Rowan pointed toward the shadowed mouth of the Murmuring Caves. Inside, the air thickened. Every sound Hedra made came back twisted. Turn back. You are too small. No one will find you. Shadows made shapes that fed her fear of being lost and alone.

Her resolve wavered. Rowan crawled from the pouch, shell a small brave lantern, and tapped a clear rhythm through the lies. He went forward.

She drew a shaky breath. “You’re right. We keep going. Light of my light.”

She sang the old songs into the echo until her own voice was the warmer thing. The whispers thinned. Through the gloom a soft pulse of light showed itself. They followed.

There the three brass stars were — not stolen, dancing, nested in the shimmering wings of Wind Sprites, creatures of laughter who had borrowed sparkle for a reel. The sprites paused, surprised.

“We did not know they were needed,” said one, voice like bells. “We only borrowed their shine.”

Hedra’s fear made room for wonder. “The village waits for Midsummer. We need them on the Banner. Your dance sounds like a wonderful thing all the same.”

A deal, then, struck without a scolding. The sprites swirled dust and returned the stars, bright and warm. They offered a little festival magic in trade. The borrowed light came home; the sprites kept their joy. That was consequence enough for play that had forgotten a village.

Hedra and Rowan went down the Whispering Hills with the stars safe in the pouch and the beetle trotting when the path allowed. The Sleepy Willows nodded a farewell that no longer tried to steal sleep. The Stream sparkled as if it had only been joking. As she descended, the old dread sat farther back, a shadow that had failed to keep up. Dawn touched the village. The Banner, lately forlorn, took the three stars and gleamed. A cheer rose from people who had feared a dark festival and received light instead. The sprites sent a breeze through the stalls, a shared delight, not a theft.

Hedra stood in that wind with Rowan on her shoulder, two who had gone as two. The longest day kept its light. Sheep bells found their ordinary music. On the peak the Banner held, and in the meadow the road-siblings rested, light of my light, under a sky that had remembered how to be midsummer.
characters: Hedra (a shepherd girl), Rowan (a stag beetle)
